fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "The People Before the Greeks", "body": "Chance opens by defining the Pelasgi through Encyclopedia Britannica as the people who occupied Greece before the twelfth century BC, the era of the Bronze Age collapse and its baffling, intricate metalwork. Homer, Herodotus and Thucydides name them in Thrace, Argos, Crete and Chalcidice, and later Greek usage applied the label to every aboriginal Aegean population. Britannica adds that surviving fifth century villages preserved a common non-Greek language, a claim Dylan flatly calls disputable, alongside the admitted uncertainty that any ancient people ever called themselves by this name at all."}, {"title": "Sailors, Storks and Grasping Straws", "body": "Chance walks through competing origins for the name. Bishop Cumberland, writing in 1794, derived it from the Greek pelagos, the sea, reading it as a word for strangers and adventurers who came by ship to settle more comfortably. Marcellus of Lesbos tied it to storks that depart and return, an etymology Aristophanes mocked in a comedy of men dressed as birds. Godfrey Higgins doubted the sailors used the name themselves. William Betham instead read Celtic roots in the Iguvine tables, where night, light, day and people combine to mean navigators who could sail by darkness as well as daylight."}, {"title": "Baal, Aplu and Letter Swaps", "body": "Much of the argument happens at the whiteboard. Dylan spells Baal in Hebrew letters and insists the ayin carries the notation that begets the Greek omicron, so the name reads closer to Bel. Chance links that syllable to Homer's verb pello, to become or come into existence, and to the British deity Belenus. Dylan shows Etruscan Aplu written right to left, ties it to Apulia in the heel of Italy, and stresses that B, P and V trade places, that Castur and Puk are exclusive to Etruria, and that C worked as G before 230 BC."}, {"title": "Tyrrhenian Towers and One Source", "body": "Dylan argues the Tyrrhenian name came from the towers and forts these people built, and that Tyre was really Tsur, phonetically close to Syrian. Thracians reached as far as the Scythians, whose priests, the korybantes and kouretes, match those of the Umbrians and Etruscans, and whom he reads as remnants of trade routes running to the Black Sea. A Latin line stating that Etruscan, Phoenician and Celtic derive from one source was his checkmate. Academics, he says, force everything westward from Mesopotamia, when Etruscan salt beds, drained swampland and the Cloaca Maxima point to Italy."}, {"title": "Dorians, Druids and Darien", "body": "Chance traces the Dorians to Dora at the foot of Mount Lebanon in Phoenicia, then plays with dory, a small flat-bottomed boat, with the Old English dorre for tower, with the French word for tower, and with Spanish toro, the bull, which loops back to Baal and to the Taurus mountains. Herodotus calls those Phoenicians something close to Dorio, a short step to druid and to the tusci, the Etruscan priests. His strongest card is Lionel Wafer, stranded among the Darien tribe in the 1600s, who learned their speech within a month because the old Irish alphabet shared the same sixteen or seventeen letters."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: We are taught that Western civilization began with the Greeks, but the linguistic evidence reveals a much older, "secret" seafaring empire that was systematically erased from our history books.
fields.Intro Paragraph 2: In this remastered episode, we decode the "Ocean Language" of the Pelasgian, the Holy Sailors who mastered the Mediterranean and the Americas long before the Bronze Age collapse. By decoding the Hebrew and Phoenician roots hidden in plain sight, we reveal why the Pelasgians were the original 'Lordly' tribe mentioned in the oldest texts. Join Chance Garton and Dylan Saccoccio as they pull back the philological veil on the true architects of our world.
